summary: Defines a data structure, a flow specification, that hosts can use to describe the quality of communication they need from the network, such as bandwidth. It was written for multimedia applications and published by the IRTF as an informational proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a video call, your computer could fill out a form saying how much speed it needs. This paper designs that form.

questions: network quality of service flow spec
how does quality of service work
subtitle: A data structure for describing network service requirements

tldr.problem: Applications like video conferencing need to tell the network about their quality requirements, such as bandwidth and acceptable delay.
tldr.mechanism: A flow specification is a standardized data structure with fields describing traffic rates, delay sensitivity, loss tolerance, and the type of guarantee requested.
tldr.outcome: This informational RFC proposes a single, flexible format that can express any flow requirement for both guaranteed and predictive services.

today: RFC 1363 is an Informational document published by the Internet Research Task Force. It was designed during the early exploration of quality of service on the Internet and has not been formally standardized or updated. While the flow spec was influential in QoS research, the Internet developed other approaches to reservations, such as RSVP (RFC 2205), which pursued similar goals through a different architecture.

sections.title: What is a Flow Specification
sections.content:
A flow specification (or flow spec) is a data structure that allows hosts to request special services from the network. Its purpose is to communicate quality of service (QoS) requirements to the internetwork so that routers and switches can make intelligent decisions about how to handle traffic.

The flow spec is designed for distributed applications like multimedia conferencing, data fusion, visualization and virtual reality, which require guarantees about the quality of communication between nodes. For example, a video conference might require a certain minimum bandwidth to ensure timely delivery of video frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like a form that a program fills out before asking the network to send data. The form says how fast the data will come, how fast it can go, and what kind of delays are okay.

sections.title: The Four Core Functions
sections.content:
A flow specification accomplishes four key tasks:

First, it characterizes how traffic will be injected into the network. This tells the network what to expect: is it a gigabit-per-second flow or a kilobit-per-second flow? The flow spec defines three traffic parameters: the sustainable rate (token bucket rate), the peak rate (maximum transmission rate), and approximate burst size (token bucket size), based in part on token bucket algorithms.

Second, it describes the application's sensitivity to delay. The minimum delay noticed field tells the network when it can stop trying to reduce delay. However, the RFC avoids letting applications specify maximum acceptable delay, since applications usually cannot know what delay is truly acceptable to end users.

Third, it expresses sensitivity to packet loss. Some applications can tolerate occasional lost packets while others cannot. Separate fields indicate overall loss sensitivity and sensitivity to burst loss (consecutive lost packets).

Finally, it indicates what quality of guarantee is needed: no guarantee, an imperfect guarantee, predicted service, or guaranteed service.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has four main questions: How fast will you send data? How much delay can you handle? How much packet loss can you tolerate? And do you need the network to promise the service will work?

sections.title: Fields in the Flow Specification
sections.content:
The flow spec is a 14-field data structure. Most fields use a 16-bit format that encodes either a precise numeric value or a well-known constant indicating a sensitivity level.

The Version field (16 bits) identifies the flow spec version; this RFC defines version 1. The Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is the largest packet the flow will send, important both for describing loss properties and for bounding transmission time on shared media.

Traffic characterization uses three fields: Token Bucket Rate (bytes per second), Token Bucket Size (bytes of burst capacity), and Maximum Transmission Rate (bytes per second peak rate). A zero token bucket rate means the application is not requesting bandwidth guarantees.

Delay sensitivity comprises Minimum Delay Noticed (microseconds, or a constant indicating no sensitivity or moderate sensitivity) and Maximum Delay Variation (microseconds between fastest and slowest expected packets). Loss sensitivity uses Loss Sensitivity, Burst Loss Sensitivity, and Loss Interval to specify acceptable loss rates.

The Quality of Guarantee field (16 bits) specifies one of six values: no guarantee, imperfect guarantee, predicted service (required or accepting imperfect), or guaranteed service (required or accepting imperfect).
sections.plainLanguage: The form has spaces for: what version this is, the biggest packet you'll send, how much speed you need, how much speed at peak, how much delay you can handle, how much delay variation is okay, how much packet loss is okay, and what type of promise you want from the network.

sections.title: Token Buckets and Traffic Shaping
sections.content:
The flow spec's traffic characterization model is based on token bucket algorithms. In the token bucket model, credits (tokens) accumulate in an imaginary bucket at a fixed rate (the token bucket rate). Each packet sent removes credits equal to its size. If insufficient credits exist, the sender must wait.

The token bucket size limits how many credits can accumulate, bounding the size of burst traffic. For example, a voice application sending at 60 kilobytes per second with a token bucket size of 30 bytes can send one burst-sized packet immediately, but must then wait for the bucket to refill.

The maximum transmission rate adds a second rate limiter: it restricts how fast successive packets can be placed on the network, preventing a single large burst from monopolizing a shared link.

The RFC emphasizes that the token bucket model is a conceptual tool; implementations may use any traffic management scheme that produces equivalent behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine tokens dropping into a bucket at a steady rate. To send a packet, you take out tokens equal to the packet's size. If the bucket is empty, you wait. A bigger bucket lets you send a bigger burst at once.

sections.title: Three Example Applications
sections.content:
The RFC provides three worked examples of flow specifications for different applications, illustrating how the fields are used in practice.

Telnet is a low-bandwidth, delay-sensitive application. A Telnet flow spec would set the token bucket rate and size to zero (no guarantee requested), set maximum delay noticed to indicate moderate sensitivity, set loss fields to indicate insensitivity, and request no guarantee. The focus is on routing around high-delay paths like satellites.

Voice over IP assumes 32 kilobit-per-second audio with 16-bit samples in UDP datagrams, yielding about 60 kilobytes per second. The spec requests that bandwidth with a 100-millisecond delay threshold, low delay variation (10 microseconds) to keep buffering small, sensitivity to loss, and predicted service (accepting imperfect guarantees).

Variable bit-rate video broadcasting at 30 frames per second with 10% average frame change and 100% worst-case change would request 8 megabits per second sustainable rate, 2 megabits per second token bucket size, 30 megabits per second peak rate, moderate delay sensitivity, one second of delay variation buffering, loss of one packet per frame, and guaranteed service only.
sections.plainLanguage: For chat (Telnet), you say "I'm not using much bandwidth but don't route me through satellites." For voice, you say "I need a steady 60 kilobytes per second and cannot wait long." For video, you say "I might burst to 30 megabits per second but average 8, and I need everything to work perfectly."

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Flow spec version (1 for this RFC).

fields.name: Maximum Transmission Unit
fields.desc: Largest packet size the flow sends.

fields.name: Token Bucket Rate
fields.desc: Sustainable data rate in bytes per second.

fields.name: Maximum Transmission Rate
fields.desc: Peak rate in bytes per second.

fields.name: Minimum Delay Noticed
fields.desc: Delay threshold below which improvements do not matter.

fields.name: Maximum Delay Variation
fields.desc: Maximum variance in delay, in microseconds.

fields.name: Loss Interval
fields.desc: Measurement interval for loss, in MTU-sized packets.
